title: The Black-Scholes formula
objectives: Use the Black-Scholes formula and explain each input
Check a price with put-call parity and code the formula

screens.title: Five inputs, one curve
screens.prose: The tree's limit has a formula. The curve is our call's value today against the share price $S$; the dashed line is its payoff at expiry. Each slider is one input. Move them and watch the curve.
screens.question: Raise the volatility $\sigma$ from 20% to 40%. What happens to the call's value at $S = 100$?

options.text: It falls, because a riskier share is worth less.
options.why: You priced the share's risk into the call. The call keeps the upside, while its downside stays capped at zero.

options.text: It does not change: volatility affects the share, not the option.
options.why: Slide $\sigma$ and watch the dot at $S = 100$. It climbs.
Value is not proportional to $\sigma$. Read the caption at 40%: about £18.02.

feedback.correct: More spread means more upside for the call.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $\sigma$ to 40% and read the caption.

explain.text: Higher $\sigma$ spreads the share's outcomes. The call gains from the spread above the strike and loses nothing extra below it, so £10.45 becomes £18.02. Of the five inputs, only $\sigma$ cannot be read off a screen.

screens.title: No time left
screens.prose: Put $\sigma$ back to 20%. Now slide $T$, the time left, down towards zero.
screens.question: What does the curve become as $T$ falls towards 0?

options.why: At expiry a call still pays: £10 if the share is at £110.

options.text: The line $S - K$, negative below the strike
options.why: A call is never worth less than zero. You need not exercise it.
You moved $T$ the wrong way. A very long-dated call creeps towards $S$; a short one does not.

hints.text: With no time left, can the share still move?
Slide $T$ to 0.01 and compare the curve with the dashed line.
With no time left the call is worth exactly what it pays.

feedback.correct: With no time left the value is the payoff.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $T$ to its smallest value and compare the two lines.

byKey.zero: At expiry a call still pays what it is in the money: £10 if the share is at £110.

explain.text: With no time left the share cannot move, so the call is worth its payoff. That is why the curve settles onto the dashed line. With a year left, the gap above the payoff is the time value.

screens.title: The formula
screens.prose: The curve is the **Black-Scholes formula**, with $\Phi$ the standard normal cdf: $$c = S\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2),$$ $$d_1 = \frac{\ln(S/K) + (r + \sigma^2/2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\quad d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt T.$$
screens.question: Work out each piece for our call.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work down the table: each line uses the ones above it.

byKey.r3c1: $d_1$ is $0.07$ divided by $\sigma\sqrt T = 0.2$. Dividing by $\sigma^2$ instead is a classic slip.

explain.text: $\ln(100/100) = 0$, so $d_1 = 0.07/0.2 = 0.35$ and $d_2 = 0.15$. Read $\Phi(d_2)$ as the risk-neutral chance the call finishes in the money. $\Phi(d_1)$ is the call's delta.

screens.title: Finishing the price
screens.prose: Read $\Phi$ from the table, then finish the price. You will need $e^{-0.05} = 0.951229$.
screens.question: Fill in each line for $d_1 = 0.35$ and $d_2 = 0.15$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look up both values, discount the strike, then subtract.

explain.text: $c = 100 \times 0.6368 - 95.12 \times 0.5596 = 10.45$. That is the 512-step tree's answer, from one line. The formula is the tree's limit as the steps shrink; we state that without proof.

screens.title: A spreadsheet slip
screens.prose: A junior's spreadsheet prices the same call at £7.72. Its lines read: $d_1 = 0.35$, $d_2 = 0.15$, $\Phi(d_1) = 0.6368$ and $\Phi(d_2) = 0.5596$.
screens.question: Which slip explains £7.72?

options.why: With $\sigma^2$ underneath, $d_1 = 0.07/0.04 = 1.75$, not the 0.35 on the sheet. The price would be £6.63.
With $T = 365$ the call is worth almost £100, the share itself. And $d_1$ would not be 0.35.

hints.text: All four lines on the sheet are right. The slip is in the last step.
The strike is paid in a year. What is it worth today?

feedback.correct: £7.72 is the price with an undiscounted strike.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The four lines are correct, so the slip is in the final subtraction.

byKey.sigma2: Putting $\sigma^2$ under $d_1$ is a real slip, but it changes $d_1$ to 1.75. This sheet shows 0.35.
byKey.days: $T$ in days is a real slip, but it sends the price near £100.
byKey.put: You matched it to the put. The put is £5.57.

explain.text: $100 \times 0.6368 - 100 \times 0.5596 = 7.72$: the strike was not discounted. It is paid in a year, so today it is worth $Ke^{-rT} = 95.12$. The other classic slips give £6.63 ($\sigma^2$ under $d_1$) and almost £100 ($T$ in days).

screens.title: The put, and parity
screens.prose: The put is $p = Ke^{-rT}\Phi(-d_2) - S\Phi(-d_1)$. Put-call parity says $c - p = S - Ke^{-rT}$. Check that the two formulas obey it, using $\Phi(-z) = 1 - \Phi(z)$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order.

lines.text: $c - p = S\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(-d_2) + S\Phi(-d_1)$, subtracting the formulas
$= S[\Phi(d_1) + \Phi(-d_1)] - Ke^{-rT}[\Phi(d_2) + \Phi(-d_2)]$, grouping the $S$ and $K$ terms

hints.text: Collect everything multiplying $S$, then everything multiplying $Ke^{-rT}$.
Each bracket is $\Phi(z) + \Phi(-z) = 1$. The numbers come last.

feedback.correct: The formulas obey parity, and the put is £5.57.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Subtract, group, simplify, then put the numbers in.

byKey.l4: The numbers need the identity $c - p = S - Ke^{-rT}$ first.

explain.text: The two brackets are each 1, so $c - p = S - Ke^{-rT}$ for any inputs. With our numbers, $p = 10.45 - 4.88 = 5.57$. Parity is a quick check on any pricer.

screens.title: The formula in code
screens.prose: `math.erf` is the error function, and $\Phi(z) = \tfrac12\left(1 + \operatorname{erf}(z/\sqrt2)\right)$. Write `norm_cdf`, then `bs_call` and `bs_put`, with $T$ in years and rates as decimals.
screens.question: Complete `norm_cdf`, `bs_call` and `bs_put`.

widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests: five options, a parity check and two values of `norm_cdf`, each compared with math.isclose.

hints.text: The put is `K * exp(-r * T) * norm_cdf(-d2) - S * norm_cdf(-d1)`.

feedback.correct: Your pricer matches the formula on every test.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare each line with the formula, and check $\sigma\sqrt T$ under $d_1$.

explain.text: The only non-obvious line is `norm_cdf`: $\Phi$ is the error function rescaled by $\sqrt 2$. Everything else is the formula as written. Parity holds to the last digit.

screens.title: What the model assumes
screens.prose: The formula is exact only inside a model of the market. Knowing its assumptions tells you where it breaks.
screens.question: Which does the Black-Scholes model assume? Select all that apply.

options.text: Volatility is constant over the option's life
Hedging is continuous and costs nothing
The share's expected return is known
options.why: You looked for growth among the inputs. The expected return never appears; you moved all five inputs.

options.text: The share price is normally distributed
options.why: Normal prices could go negative. The model makes log prices normal.
Pricing uses risk-neutral probabilities, but nobody has to be risk-neutral. The hedge argument works for anyone.

hints.text: Think back to the tree: what did it need, and what never entered?
The tree used one $\sigma$ for every step, and it rehedged at every step.
Constant $\sigma$, lognormal prices, no jumps and continuous hedging. Growth never entered.

feedback.correct: Four assumptions, and expected growth is not one of them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep what the tree needed, and drop what never entered the formula.

byKey.mu: You looked for growth among the inputs. The expected return never appears in the formula.

explain.text: The model needs constant $\sigma$, lognormal prices, no jumps and continuous, costless hedging. In markets, options at different strikes imply different $\sigma$: the **smile**, in the next lesson. Discrete hedging and jumps come in the last lesson of this level.

screens.title: Delta from the formula
screens.prose: The formula's slopes are the Greeks (options, How the price responds). Delta, the slope against $S$, is $\Phi(d_1)$ for a call. A desk has sold 1,000 of our calls and wants to be flat against small moves.
screens.question: How many shares should the desk hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply delta per call by the number of calls.

byKey.one: You hedged one share per call. That is the slope of the payoff deep in the money at expiry, not today's slope.
byKey.d2: You used $\Phi(d_2)$, the in-the-money chance. Delta is $\Phi(d_1)$.
byKey.put: 0.363 is the size of the put's delta, $1 - \Phi(d_1)$.
byKey.half: An at-the-money call's delta is not exactly a half. Here it is 0.6368.

explain.text: Delta is $\Phi(0.35) = 0.6368$, the tangent's slope, so 637 shares. Gamma says how fast delta moves with $S$: 0.0188 here. Vega is the change for one vol point (£0.38), theta the decay per day (about −£0.018), rho the change with $r$.

screens.title: A put for a client
screens.prose: A client wants a 3-month put on a share at £50, struck at £48. The desk uses $r = 4\%$ and $\sigma = 30\%$, so $T = 0.25$. You find $d_1 = 0.4138$ and $d_2 = 0.2638$, with $\Phi(-d_1) = 0.3395$ and $\Phi(-d_2) = 0.3960$.
screens.question: What should the desk charge for the put, before any margin?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Discount the strike, then use $\Phi(-d_2)$ and $\Phi(-d_1)$.

byKey.nodisc: You used £48 undiscounted. The strike is paid in 3 months, so use $48e^{-0.01}$.
byKey.signs: A negative price means you used $\Phi(d_1)$ and $\Phi(d_2)$. The put needs $\Phi(-d_1)$ and $\Phi(-d_2)$.

explain.text: $p = 47.52 \times 0.3960 - 50 \times 0.3395 = 1.84$. With $T = 90$ entered in days the sheet would show £0.56. The put's delta is $\Phi(d_1) - 1 = -0.34$, so the desk hedges by shorting 0.34 shares per put.

ideas: Black-Scholes is the many-step tree in one line: $c = S\Phi(d_1) - Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2)$, £10.45 for our call.
Price rises with $S$, $\sigma$, $T$ and $r$ and falls with $K$; as $T \to 0$ it becomes the payoff, as $\sigma \to 0$ it becomes $\max(S - Ke^{-rT}, 0)$.
The model assumes constant volatility, lognormal prices, no jumps and continuous hedging. Delta is $\Phi(d_1)$.

formula.name: Black-Scholes
formula.note: $T$ in years; $\sigma\sqrt T$, not $\sigma^2$, underneath; discount the strike.

summary.trap: Forgetting $e^{-rT}$ on the strike turns £10.45 into £7.72.

quiz.prose: Take our call ($S = K = 100$, $r = 5\%$, $T = 1$) and let $\sigma$ fall almost to zero.
quiz.question: What is the call worth in the limit?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With no volatility the share grows at $r$ for sure.

byKey.zero: You used the payoff today, $\max(100 - 100, 0)$. The share grows at $r$, so it ends at $100e^{0.05}$.
byKey.bs: That is the price at 20% volatility.

explain.text: With $\sigma = 0$ the share ends at $100e^{0.05} = 105.13$ for sure. The call pays £5.13 in a year, worth $5.13e^{-0.05} = 4.88$ today. That is $\max(S - Ke^{-rT}, 0)$.

quiz.prose: Hold $S$, $K$, $\sigma$ and $T$ fixed and raise $r$ from 5% to 8%.
quiz.question: What happens to the call's price?

options.text: It rises: the strike, paid later, is worth less today
It falls: future payoffs are discounted more
options.why: You discounted the payoff but forgot the strike. The call holder pays $K$ later, and that is the bigger effect.

options.text: No change: the rate only matters for bonds
options.why: $r$ appears twice in the formula, in $d_1$ and in $Ke^{-rT}$.

feedback.correct: A higher rate shrinks $Ke^{-rT}$, so the call rises.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the $Ke^{-rT}$ term.

explain.text: At 8% the call is worth £12.11 against £10.45. The strike's present value falls from £95.12 to £92.31.

quiz.prose: A share is at £110, the strike is £100, $r = 0$, $\sigma = 25\%$ and $T = 4$ years.
quiz.question: What is $d_1$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The denominator is $\sigma\sqrt T = 0.25 \times 2$.

byKey.sig2: You divided by $\sigma^2\sqrt T$. The denominator is $\sigma\sqrt T$.
byKey.nosqrt: You divided by $\sigma$ alone. The denominator is $\sigma\sqrt T = 0.5$.

explain.text: $\ln 1.1 = 0.0953$ and $(\sigma^2/2)T = 0.03125 \times 4 = 0.125$. The sum 0.2203 over $\sigma\sqrt T = 0.5$ gives 0.4406.

quiz.prose: A 6-month call on a £50 share, struck at £52, costs £6.00. The rate is $r = 4\%$, so $Ke^{-rT} = 52e^{-0.02} = 50.97$.
quiz.question: What must the matching put cost?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rearrange $c - p = S - Ke^{-rT}$.

byKey.sign: You added $S - Ke^{-rT}$ instead of subtracting it. Rearrange $c - p = S - Ke^{-rT}$ for $p$.

explain.text: $p = 6.00 - 50 + 50.97 = 6.97$. The put costs more than the call because the strike is above the share's forward price.
